theme: LORD, you were favorable to your land
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 85. It is a prayer for revival that remembers past forgiveness and looks for a future where righteousness and peace meet. Read verses 10 to 13 slowly.
settingTheScene: Psalm 85 is a psalm of the sons of Korah. It begins by recalling that God has restored the fortunes of Jacob, and then asks him to do it again. It may have been written after the return from Babylon, when the people were back in the land but the glory had not returned. It will be read again in Unit 14 with an emphasis on the return. Here it is a prayer from the dark side of the exile, asking God to revive his people.
observation: “LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob” (v. 1).
“You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin” (v. 2).
“Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!” (v. 4).
“Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (v. 6).
“Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation” (v. 7).
“Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other” (v. 10).
“Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky” (v. 11).
“Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with memory: God has been favorable before. He forgave and covered sin and turned away from his fierce anger. This past mercy is the basis of the plea. When we do not know what to pray, we can start by recalling what God has already done.

The prayer is for revival. “Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” Joy in God is the goal. Revival here is not an event or a program but a renewal of the people’s delight in the LORD. It assumes that left alone, we dry out.

Then the psalmist does something striking. He says, “Let me hear what God the LORD will speak.” He stops talking and listens. And the word that comes is peace, for those who turn their hearts to him. God’s salvation is near to those who fear him, “that glory may dwell in our land.”

The center of the psalm is its beautiful picture in verses 10 and 11. Four qualities, which usually seem to pull against each other, are brought together: steadfast love and faithfulness, righteousness and peace. They meet and kiss. This is a picture of the gospel. How can God be both loving and just? How can he bring peace without compromising righteousness? In the cross, these meet. Steadfast love forgives, and faithfulness keeps the promise to punish sin. Righteousness is satisfied, and peace is made.

The psalm ends with the hope of the Lord’s appearance: “Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.” The good that will come will come from heaven and from the earth together.
connection: Romans 3:25-26 shows how God is both just and the justifier, where love and righteousness meet. Colossians 1:20 says that God was pleased “to reconcile to himself all things, making peace by the blood of his cross.” Romans 5:1 says that we have peace with God. John 1:14 says that the Word became flesh, full of grace and truth. Luke 2:14 announces “peace among those with whom he is pleased.”
application:
Make a list of the ways God has been “favorable to your land” in your life.

Pray “Will you not revive us again?” for your church and for yourself.

Sit in silence and say, “Let me hear what God the LORD will speak.” Listen for a few minutes.
prayerPrompts: Tell him you want steadfast love and faithfulness to meet in your life.
